239.title: A teacher and a friend (Avot 1:6)
239.hook: get yourself a teacher, gain a companion, and judge everyone favorably
239.carry: judge on the side of merit
239.howItsDone: Traditional Jewish study is often done in a chavruta, a pair of study partners who read and argue together, and dan lechaf zechut, judging others favorably, is counted among the everyday duties between people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a house open wide, where the poor are members of the household. Your line was open the door wide. Did you plan an invitation? Today, the next pair of teachers, and three things everyone needs. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

A friend texts, I need to talk, and then goes silent for six hours. A coworker walks past without saying hi. Your brother forgets your birthday. In each case, your brain writes a story in about half a second. They're angry at me. They're rude. He doesn't care. Sometimes the story is right. Often, it isn't. The phone died. She was crying in the stairwell. He's drowning at work. The next teacher in Avot's chain, Joshua ben Perachyah, gives three pieces of advice. The last one is about that story in your head.
screen: `I NEED TO TALK. THEN SILENCE.` → `THE STORY IN HALF A SECOND.` → `JOSHUA BEN PERACHYAH.`

segments.voice: Joshua ben Perachyah says, in paraphrase: make for yourself a teacher, acquire for yourself a friend, and judge every person favorably. Look at the verbs. Make a teacher. Not find one; make one. Even if no perfect teacher appears, choose someone and make them your teacher. Then, acquire a friend. The Hebrew kneh means buy. A real friend costs you something: time, patience, the humility to be corrected. An early companion to Avot says a true friend is someone you eat with, study with, and trust with your secrets. Jewish learning built this into its method. Students study in pairs, a chavruta, arguing over every line. Now the third: judge every person favorably. In Hebrew, lechaf zechut, on the side of merit. Picture a scale. When you don't know why someone did something, tip it toward the good reading. The Talmud tells a story about it. A man works three years for a farmer. On the eve of the holiday he asks for his wages. No money, the farmer says. Then give me produce. I don't have any. Land? Cattle? Blankets? None. The worker goes home empty-handed. After the holiday the farmer arrives with his wages and gifts, and asks: what did you think when I said I had nothing? Each time, the worker had imagined an innocent reason. And he was right: the farmer had pledged all his property to the Temple, and had it undone. The farmer says: as you judged me favorably, may God judge you favorably.
screen: `MAKE YOURSELF A TEACHER.` · `ACQUIRE A FRIEND.` · `LECHAF ZECHUT — ON THE SIDE OF MERIT.` · `THE WORKER WHO WASN'T PAID.` · then, large: `JUDGE ON THE SIDE OF MERIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: assume the best of someone today. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose behavior bothered you recently. Picture the moment. Now, like the worker, come up with an innocent explanation. Then a second one. Then a third. You don't have to believe them. Just notice there's more than one story. Let the scale tip, a little, toward merit. The bell holds the time.
A teacher and a friend. Joshua ben Perachyah's saying in Avot: make yourself a teacher, acquire a friend, and judge every person on the side of merit.
screen: `A TEACHER AND A FRIEND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: judge on the side of merit. Today, when someone lets you down, come up with one innocent reason before you react. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

in the Talmud's story, the farmer really had no money

Avot says to wait for the perfect teacher to find you
it says make yourself a teacher: choose one.

options: he's cheating me.
there must be a reason I don't know.

fork.reveal: in the Talmud's story, the worker imagined an innocent reason each time, and was right. the farmer said: as you judged me favorably, may God judge you favorably.

trapdoor: what you thought: give people the benefit of the doubt.
what it means: tip the scale toward merit when you don't know someone's reasons, and seek out a teacher and a friend who will help you see.
what a scholar hears: kaf is the pan of a scale, zechut is merit; the Talmud's story of the unpaid worker (Shabbat 127b) is the classic illustration.

240.title: Choose your neighbors (Avot 1:7)
240.hook: Nittai: keep far from a bad neighbor, and don't give up on justice
240.howItsDone: Jewish tradition gives weight to choosing one's community and surroundings, and many Jews weigh the neighborhood, school and friends around them with Nittai's advice in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a teacher and a friend: Joshua ben Perachyah said make a teacher, acquire a friend, and judge on the side of merit. Did you find an innocent reason for someone? Today, his partner, Nittai, adds the other side. Day two hundred forty.

You've probably noticed it. Spend a week with a friend who complains about everything, and you start complaining too. Sit near the coworker who cuts corners, and your corners start getting shorter. Scroll a certain feed for an hour, and you come away a little meaner than you went in. We catch moods and habits from the people around us, the way we catch colds. Yesterday, Joshua ben Perachyah told us to judge everyone favorably. Today his teaching partner, Nittai of Arbel, answers with a warning. Being generous about people doesn't mean living next door to everything.
screen: `WE CATCH HABITS LIKE COLDS.` → `A LITTLE MEANER THAN BEFORE.` → `NITTAI OF ARBEL.`

segments.voice: Nittai of Arbel says three things, in paraphrase. Keep far from a bad neighbor. Don't attach yourself to a wicked person. And don't give up on justice; or, more literally, don't despair of retribution. Start with the neighbor. In the ancient world, you couldn't easily move. So the advice was practical: when you choose where to live, who to work beside, who to be close to, choose with care. Rashi, reading a detail in the book of Numbers, notices who camped next to whom in the desert. The tribe camped beside a famous rebel was drawn into his rebellion. The tribes camped beside Moses grew great in learning. And Rashi passes on a saying: woe to the wicked, and woe to his neighbor; good for the righteous, and good for his neighbor. Notice these two sayings sit side by side in Avot, from a pair of teachers. Judge everyone favorably. Keep far from a bad neighbor. Both are true. You can give someone the benefit of the doubt and still choose not to sit next to them every day. Kindness isn't the same as closeness. Then the third line. Don't despair of retribution. Commentators hear it two ways. Don't envy people who seem to get away with harm; justice isn't finished yet. And don't get complacent yourself when things go well; nobody's beyond consequences. Either way, the world has a moral shape, even when it's hard to see. Choose who you live near, and don't give up on that shape.
screen: `KEEP FAR FROM A BAD NEIGHBOR.` · `WOE TO THE WICKED AND HIS NEIGHBOR.` · `KINDNESS ISN'T CLOSENESS.` · `DON'T GIVE UP ON JUSTICE.` · then, large: `CHOOSE YOUR NEIGHBORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: step back from one bad influence. Settle, and breathe. Think about what you're close to every day: people, places, feeds, habits, group chats. Is there one that reliably leaves you worse? Not a person to condemn, just a neighbor to move away from. Picture putting a little distance there: muting it, sitting elsewhere, spending the time somewhere better. And think of one good neighbor to move toward. The bell holds the time.
Choose your neighbors. Nittai of Arbel's saying in Avot: keep far from a bad neighbor, don't join the wicked, and don't give up on justice.
Your line: choose your neighbors. Today, put a little distance between you and one thing that makes you worse, and move a little closer to one that makes you better. Day two hundred forty.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't live next to bad people.
what it means: choose carefully who and what you stay close to, and don't give up on justice.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on Numbers 3 notes the tribe camped beside Korah joined his rebellion, while the tribes beside Moses grew in learning: woe to the wicked and woe to his neighbor.

241.title: Careful words (Avot 1:9)
241.hook: Simeon ben Shetach: question witnesses well, and guard your words so no one learns to lie
241.howItsDone: Jewish law built strict rules for testimony on this teaching: witnesses are questioned separately and closely, and many Jews read Avot 1:9 as a guide to honest speech well beyond the courtroom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nittai of Arbel: keep far from a bad neighbor, and don't give up on justice. Your line was choose your neighbors. Did you step back from one bad influence? Day two hundred forty-one.

A kid is standing in the kitchen with crumbs on his shirt, and a parent asks, you didn't take the last cookie, did you? And the kid, who is not a fool, says no. Notice what happened. The question handed him the answer. It told him which story would get him out of trouble. Most of us ask questions like that every week, at home, at work, in a group chat. Two thousand years ago, a judge in Jerusalem noticed the same thing in a courtroom, where the stakes were a lot higher than a cookie. Today: careful words.
screen: `CRUMBS ON HIS SHIRT.` → `THE QUESTION HANDED HIM THE ANSWER.` → `A JUDGE IN JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: The judge is Simeon ben Shetach, one of the pairs of teachers who carry the chain of Pirkei Avot through the last century before the Common Era. He led the court in a stormy time, and later tradition remembers him as fearless in front of kings. His saying, in chapter one, comes in two halves. First: examine the witnesses thoroughly. The Torah says a matter is established by two or three witnesses, and Simeon wants them questioned hard, because a careless court convicts the innocent. Then the second half, which is the surprising one: and be careful with your words, so that they don't learn from them to lie. That half isn't aimed at the witnesses. It's aimed at the judge. If the judge asks, was the knife in his right hand, the witness now knows the court is looking for a knife in a right hand. The question teaches the lie. So the careful judge asks open questions, and lets the story come out on its own. The Talmud tells a story about Simeon that shows how seriously he took this. He once saw a man chase another man into a ruin. He ran in after them and found one man dying and the other holding a bloody sword. And Simeon said, in effect: either you killed him, or I did. But I can't convict you. The Torah needs two witnesses, and I only saw the sword, not the blow. Even when he was sure, he held his own words to the standard he set for everyone else. That's the idea for today. Our questions shape what people tell us, and what we say we saw becomes someone else's truth.
screen: `SIMEON BEN SHETACH, A JUDGE.` · `QUESTION THE WITNESSES WELL.` · `YOUR QUESTION CAN TEACH THE LIE.` · `THE SWORD IN THE RUIN.` · then, large: `CAREFUL WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse one open question. Settle, and breathe. Think of a conversation you'll have today where you want the truth. With a child, a coworker, a friend. Notice the question you'd normally ask, the one with the answer tucked inside it. Now, slowly, turn it into an open one. Not, you finished it, right? Just, how did it go? Say it silently a few times, until it feels natural. The bell holds the time.
Careful words. Simeon ben Shetach's warning to judges: the way you ask can teach someone how to lie.
Your line: careful words. Today, when you want to know what really happened, ask an open question and then stop talking. Day two hundred forty-one.

what a scholar hears: many classic commentators read the warning as addressed to the judge, whose leading questions shape the testimony.

242.title: Love the work (Avot 1:10)
242.hook: Shemaiah: love labor, hate lording over others, don't court the powerful
242.howItsDone: Many Jews read Avot 1:10 as a teaching about the dignity of work, and the sages of the Mishnah and Talmud are remembered as people with trades as well as teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon ben Shetach, the judge who knew a question can teach a lie. Your line was careful words. Did you ask one open question? Day two hundred forty-two.

A winter Friday in Jerusalem, a long time ago. A poor young laborer has spent half his day's wage to get into the house of study, and today he has nothing left, so the guard won't let him in. He climbs onto the roof and lies down by the skylight, just to hear the teachers talk. Snow begins to fall. He stays. In the morning, the two teachers inside notice the room is strangely dark. They look up and find a man buried in snow across the window. The Talmud says they carried him down, warmed him by the fire, and said he was worth it. The young man was Hillel. And one of his teachers was Shemaiah.
screen: `A WINTER FRIDAY.` → `HILLEL ON THE ROOF.` → `SHEMAIAH INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Shemaiah and his partner Avtalyon are the next pair in the chain of Pirkei Avot, and the Talmud remembers that they came from families of converts, yet they led the sages of their day. Shemaiah's saying has three short parts. First: love work. The Hebrew word is melakhah, the same word used for the creative work that stops on Shabbat. Not just tolerate your job. Love it. Many of the sages had trades. They were sandal makers, farmers, laborers, and they didn't see work as a distraction from a holy life. It was part of one. Second: hate rabbanut. It sounds like being a rabbi, but here it means lording it over people, holding a title so others have to bow. Shemaiah had authority, and he warns against loving it. Third: don't get too close to the ruling power. The rulers of his time could be dangerous, and later commentators say they draw you close when it suits them and drop you when it doesn't. Put the three together and you get a picture of a healthy life: honest work, done gladly, without climbing over people, and without selling yourself to whoever's in charge. Now go back to the roof. Hillel spent half of every wage just to be let in to learn. He loved the work, both kinds: the labor that paid the fee, and the learning it paid for. And the teachers who found him didn't hand him a title. They warmed him up.
screen: `SHEMAIAH AND AVTALYON.` · `LOVE WORK: MELAKHAH.` · `HATE LORDING IT OVER OTHERS.` · `DON'T COURT THE POWERFUL.` · then, large: `LOVE THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the part of your work you can love. Settle, and breathe. Picture a task waiting for you today: a report, a sink of dishes, a shift, homework. Don't picture the whole mountain. Find one small piece of it that's honestly good. The feel of a clean counter. A problem that clicks. A customer you helped. Hold that piece in your mind, and let yourself be glad of it. The bell holds the time.
Love the work. Shemaiah's teaching: honest labor done gladly, with no lording it over others and no chasing the powerful.
Your line: love the work. Today, do one ordinary task a little more carefully than you need to, and notice if it feels different. Day two hundred forty-two.

243.title: Love peace, pursue peace (Avot 1:12)
243.hook: Hillel: be a disciple of Aaron, loving peace, loving people, drawing them near
243.howItsDone: Many Jews point to Aaron as the model peacemaker, and making peace between people (hava'at shalom) is counted among the good deeds whose fruits a person enjoys in this world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemaiah, and Hillel lying in the snow by the skylight. Your line was love the work. Which ordinary task did you do with care? Today, that young man on the roof grows up. Day two hundred forty-three.

Two friends have stopped talking. Maybe it was a wedding seating chart, maybe money, maybe one sharp text. You're friends with both of them, and you know the silence is hurting them both. Most of us do one of two things here. We pick a side, or we carefully stay out of it. Pirkei Avot now reaches the most quoted teacher in the whole tractate, the poor laborer from the roof, all grown up. He's the last of the great pairs in the chain, alongside a sage named Shammai. And his first saying is about exactly this moment: two people who won't speak, and someone in the middle.
screen: `TWO FRIENDS, NOT TALKING.` → `PICK A SIDE, OR STAY OUT?` → `HILLEL.`

segments.voice: Hillel came to the land of Israel from Babylonia, poor and hungry to learn, and later tradition remembers him as the gentlest of the sages. His saying begins: be one of the disciples of Aaron. Aaron, Moses's brother, the first high priest. Then Hillel says what kind of disciple: loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and drawing them near to the Torah. Why Aaron? The Torah never tells a story of Aaron making peace. The rabbis filled that silence. An early collection called Avot of Rabbi Natan says that when two people quarreled, Aaron would go and sit with one of them and say, your friend is heartbroken, he's ashamed of what he did to you. Then he would go to the other and say the same thing. And when the two met, they would embrace. Notice the verbs. Loving peace is a feeling. Pursuing peace is a chase. The Hebrew word is rodef, the word for running after something. Hillel may be echoing the psalm, which in the old King James wording says, "Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it." Peace doesn't come looking for you. You go out after it, like Aaron walking from one house to the other. And then the last part: love people, and draw them near. Hillel uses a word that means all creatures, every human being, not only the ones who already agree with you. He doesn't say push them toward the Torah. He says bring them close. That's the picture of a disciple of Aaron: someone who walks between people until they can find each other again.
screen: `BE A DISCIPLE OF AARON.` · `AARON WALKS BETWEEN TWO HOUSES.` · `RODEF: PEACE IS A CHASE.` · `LOVE PEOPLE, DRAW THEM NEAR.` · then, large: `SEEK PEACE, AND PURSUE IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the two people. Settle, and breathe. Think of two people in your life who aren't getting along. Family, coworkers, friends. Hold one of them in mind, and remember something good about them. Then the other. Now ask what one small, true thing you could say to either of them that would make the other seem a little more human. Don't plan a big speech. One sentence, like Aaron's. If you pray, you can hold them both before God. The bell holds the time.
Hillel. The sage from Babylonia who said: be a disciple of Aaron, love peace and chase it, love people and draw them near.
Your line: pursue peace. Today, say one kind, true word about someone to a person who's upset with them. Day two hundred forty-three.

244.title: If not now, when? (Avot 1:14)
244.hook: Hillel: if I am not for myself, who is; if only for myself, what am I; if not now, when
244.howItsDone: Hillel's three questions are among the best-known lines of Pirkei Avot, studied on summer Shabbat afternoons and often quoted in Jewish teaching as a call to act without delay.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel told us to be disciples of Aaron, walking between two people until they meet. Your line was pursue peace. Did you carry a kind word across? Day two hundred forty-four.

There's a thing on your list that's been there for weeks. The call to your grandmother. The doctor's appointment. The apology. The form. Every morning it slides down to tomorrow, and tomorrow is always a better day for it. Two thousand years ago, Hillel wrote the shortest possible answer to that list. It's three questions, one line each, and it may be the most quoted sentence in all of Pirkei Avot. People have put it on posters, in speeches, and on the title page of novels. The last question is only four words in English. You probably already know it.
screen: `THE THING ON YOUR LIST.` → `TOMORROW IS ALWAYS BETTER.` → `THREE QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Here is Hillel's saying, in chapter one. If I am not for myself, who will be for me? And when I am for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? Take them one at a time. The first question is about responsibility. Nobody else can live your life, learn your lessons, or do your good deeds for you. Commentators read it this way: if I don't work on myself, no one can do it in my place. It's not selfish. It's a person standing up. The second question turns right around. And when I am only for myself, what am I? A person who lives only for himself shrinks. Hillel doesn't answer the question. He lets it sit there, a little uncomfortable, and lets you fill it in. So the first two lines hold each other in balance. Stand up for yourself. Don't stop there. And then the third line, which gives both of them a deadline. If not now, when? The Hebrew is im lo akhshav, eimatai. Akhshav is the ordinary word for now, the one people use to call a kid to dinner. There's no poetry in it. It means this minute. Some commentators add a sharper reading: now means this life, this world, while you still have time to act. The saying works like a staircase. Care for yourself. Care beyond yourself. Start today. Hillel, who climbed onto a roof in the snow rather than miss one lesson, knew what it meant to not wait for a better day.
screen: `IF I AM NOT FOR MYSELF, WHO?` · `IF ONLY FOR MYSELF, WHAT AM I?` · `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?` · `AKHSHAV: THIS MINUTE.` · then, large: `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the delayed thing. Settle, and breathe. Let the list in your head come up, and notice which item has been waiting longest. Don't judge yourself for it. Just look at it. Now make it smaller: what's the very first step, the one that takes two minutes? Opening the email. Finding the number. Writing the first line. Picture yourself doing just that step, right after the bell. The bell holds the time.
If not now. The last of Hillel's three questions: care for yourself, care beyond yourself, and don't wait for a better day.
Your line: if not now, when. Today, take the first two-minute step on one thing you've been putting off. Day two hundred forty-four.

245.title: Say little, do much (Avot 1:15)
245.hook: Shammai: make study regular, say little and do much, greet everyone cheerfully
245.howItsDone: Many Jews keep a fixed daily or weekly time for Torah study, often with a study partner, and 'receive everyone with a cheerful face' is taught as basic Jewish courtesy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel's three questions, ending with four famous words. Your line was if not now, when. Did you take the first small step? Today, Hillel's partner. Day two hundred forty-five.

You know two kinds of people. One says, I'll bring a little something, and walks in with a tray of food that feeds the whole party. The other promises the moon in the group chat, and shows up with a bag of ice. Today's sage is Shammai, the partner of Hillel in the chain. Later stories give him a reputation as the strict one, the one with the short temper, and you'll meet one of those stories in a few weeks. So his saying is a surprise. Because it ends with a smile.
screen: `A LITTLE SOMETHING, A WHOLE TRAY.` → `SHAMMAI, THE STRICT ONE.` → `A SAYING THAT ENDS WITH A SMILE.`

segments.voice: Shammai's saying has three parts. First: make your Torah fixed. Set a regular time for study, and keep it, instead of learning only when you happen to feel like it. Second: say little and do much. The Talmud finds the model for this in Abraham. Three strangers come to his tent in the heat of the day, and he offers them, in his words, just a morsel of bread. Then he runs to the herd for a tender calf, has cakes baked from fine flour, and brings curd and milk. He promised a snack and served a feast. The rabbis say that's how the righteous behave: they promise a little and do a lot. Third, and this is the surprise from the strict one: receive every person with a cheerful face. The Hebrew is be'sever panim yafot, literally with a pleasant, beautiful face. Every person. Not only your friends, not only the important ones. An early rabbinic collection takes it even further: give someone the best gifts in the world with a sour face, and it's as if you gave nothing; greet them warmly with empty hands, and it's as if you gave them everything. Put all three together: a steady habit, quiet follow-through, and a warm face at the door. And that closes a week of sages: judge people favorably, choose your neighbors, careful words, love the work, pursue peace, if not now when, and today, say little, do much.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: warm up your face. It sounds silly. Try it anyway. Settle, and breathe. Notice what your face is doing right now. Probably nothing much, or a little tight around the eyes. Let your jaw loosen. Let your forehead go soft. Now think of the next person you'll see today, and picture greeting them the way you'd greet someone you've missed. Just hold that picture, and let the warmth reach your face. The bell holds the time.
Say little. Shammai's rule, learned from Abraham: promise a little, do a lot, and greet every person with a cheerful face.
Your line: say little, do much. Today, do one kind thing without announcing it first, and greet everyone you meet with a real smile. Day two hundred forty-five.
